output.title: When glossary upkeep turns into a workflow decision
output.body:
Glossary upkeep stops being useful when it is no longer a simple repeatable task and starts becoming a judgement call that steals time from the rest of the business.

If you are running a small company, the first question is not “can AI touch this?” It is: does this glossary get updated often enough, and by the same rule each time, that a person keeps re-checking the same terms? If the answer is no, automation will probably just add another layer of maintenance.

A better next step is to map one week of glossary work in plain English: where each change comes from, who decides whether it should be published, and what the owner must approve before it goes live. Keep that human approval rule explicit. Bareni’s work stays inside the customer’s own environment, but published content still needs an owner decision.

If the glossary source is a digital system you can reach through a database, API, or export, that is a workable starting point. If it is paper-heavy or depends on scan/OCR handling, that is outside current scope. In that case, the honest answer may be to keep it manual for now. Sometimes the least exciting option is the right one.
